title: Embryo, Cotyledons, Radicle, Hypocotyl, and Plumule
objective: Trace the embryo structures that become the early root and shoot system.

terms.definition: The young sporophyte contained within the seed.
An embryonic leaf that stores or transfers reserves and becomes photosynthetic after emergence.
The embryonic root that normally emerges first during germination.
The embryonic stem region below the cotyledons.
The embryonic shoot region containing the shoot apex and earliest leaf primordia.

coreScience: The cannabis embryo is a compact plant body prepared to resume growth when water, temperature, oxygen, and viability permit. The radicle is the first obvious organ to extend. Its emergence marks germination in many seed-testing definitions. The radicle anchors the seedling and develops into the initial root axis, from which lateral roots and absorbing surfaces expand.

The hypocotyl elongates and helps lift the cotyledons during emergence. The two cotyledons open above the medium, become green, and contribute photosynthesis while the first true leaves expand. Cotyledons are not the first true leaves: they are embryo structures with a simpler shape and a different developmental origin.

The shoot apex between the cotyledons produces the first true leaves and subsequent stem nodes. Radicle injury, constriction around the hypocotyl, persistent seed coverings, or oxygen depletion in saturated media can interrupt emergence. Salinity and disease can also impair establishment, but they require their own measurements and evidence rather than being inferred from a stalled seedling.

Germination begins physiologically before the radicle becomes visible. Water uptake rehydrates tissues, restores membrane organization, activates metabolism, and supports mobilization of stored reserves. Respiration supplies energy for cell expansion and growth, which makes oxygen availability important in a saturated or poorly aerated medium. The visible radicle is therefore the outcome of earlier metabolic events, and failure to emerge can result from loss of viability or from environmental conditions that prevent those processes from progressing normally.
cultivationRelevance: Perfect manual orientation is less important than avoiding radicle injury. Roots generally reorient through gravitropism, but handling method, developmental stage, and physical obstruction affect the outcome; long exposed radicles are especially easy to damage.
Score emergence by structure: radicle appearance, cotyledon opening, first true leaves, and normal root-shoot balance. Do not call every emerged seedling healthy.

During handling, prioritize protection of the emerging radicle and the hypocotyl-root transition. Once the radicle extends, bending, pinching, drying, or abrasion can damage the root meristem or conductive tissues before the seedling has redundancy. If pre-germination is used, transfer methods should minimize time exposed to dry air and mechanical contact.

Use structural abnormalities to guide troubleshooting rather than assigning a single cause from appearance. Delayed radicle emergence, trapped cotyledons, hypocotyl collapse, root-tip necrosis, asymmetric true leaves, or stalled growth can result from different combinations of seed vigor, moisture, oxygen, salinity, temperature, pathogens, mechanical barriers, or handling. Record the pattern and environment before correcting it.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record lot ID, number started, method, medium, moisture method, temperature, start date/time, and the criterion used to define germination. This establishes the denominator for later normal-seedling and abnormal-seedling rates.

Record time to first radicle emergence and, for representative samples, approximate length or developmental class. Note discoloration, tip injury, abnormal direction only when physically constrained, or arrested extension.

Record emergence date, hypocotyl orientation, excessive elongation, constriction, collapse, lesions, or mechanical damage. Pair abnormalities with media depth, moisture, temperature, light-on-emergence, and handling records.

Record whether cotyledons open fully, remain trapped by fruit/seed tissues, are damaged, discolored, asymmetric, or fail to expand. Do not score a seedling as normal solely because it reached the surface.

Record date the first true leaves are visible, symmetry, distortion, apex damage, and subsequent node development. Persistent abnormalities should be linked to environmental, nutritional, pest, disease, or genetic follow-up rather than diagnosed from one image.

At transplant or diagnostic sampling, record root length/distribution, new root tips, shoot size, and whether both systems are advancing. Coordinated development is a stronger establishment indicator than emergence alone.

misconceptions: The first two round leaves are true leaves: They are cotyledons.
The emerging radicle should be green: It is embryonic root tissue and is typically pale before light exposure or abnormal greening.
A seedling that breaks the surface has passed: Normal development requires coordinated roots, hypocotyl, cotyledons, and shoot apex.
evidenceLimits: The structural sequence from embryo activation through radicle emergence, hypocotyl extension, cotyledon expansion, and true-leaf development is transferable, but exact timing varies with seed lot, temperature, water availability, oxygen, salinity, microbial pressure, and handling. Abnormal morphology is descriptive evidence, not a unique diagnosis; several stresses can produce similar seedling outcomes and require environmental or laboratory confirmation.
